name: Joint stacking / centration

card.summary: A lifting-technique idea of keeping joints aligned and centred under load, so training stays comfortable and consistent and builds the physique over time.

quick.overview:
Joint stacking, or centration, is the idea that a joint should sit centred and aligned when a load passes through it, for example the ball of the shoulder sitting in the socket during a press. Lifters use the phrase to describe lining up wrists, elbows and shoulders, or knees and hips, under the bar.

For looks, the connection is through training: proponents say well-aligned lifting is more comfortable, lets people train harder and longer, and so supports muscle building.
quick.how: Lifters describe it as checking positions during warm-ups and working sets, often with coaching or video. It is a technique focus within normal training rather than a product.
quick.risks: No specific harms are documented for the concept itself. Orthopaedic papers on joint centration concern clinical conditions such as shoulder and hip problems, not gym technique [1][2].

lead: In orthopaedics, "centration" refers to a joint head sitting centred in its socket. Studies describe humeral head centration at the shoulder, which is influenced by the shape and orientation of the glenoid [1]. Hip microinstability in athletes has also been reported in case literature [2].

In strength training communities the phrase "joint stacking" is used loosely for keeping joints aligned under load. The concept is used to train with comfortable positions, which supporters link to consistent training and muscle development, a chain toward a better physique.

angle.text: Lifters use alignment cues to keep training comfortable, and so to keep building muscle.

paras: Research on shoulder stability reports that glenoid retroversion is an important factor for humeral head centration and posterior stability [1]. A case report describes microinstability of the hip in a collegiate endurance athlete [2].
Gym use of the term is informal. This entry covers the concept; it does not prescribe technique.
No studies found on joint stacking as a gym technique. Orthopaedic studies of centration in patients exist [1][2].
